strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely question: why reward-filtered iterative self-improvement can work in finite-sample regimes, and when easy-to-hard curricula can help. The task-centric framing is useful and more aligned with verifier-based reasoning pipelines than some prior population-level accounts.

The theoretical development is substantial. The single-step analysis makes explicit the role of acceptance rates, finite accepted sample size, and per-question sampling budget, and the multi-step map gives a clear way to reason about monotonic improvement and saturation.

The curriculum section provides interpretable sufficient conditions involving task difficulty separation, sample budget, and initialization quality. Even if restrictive, these conditions give concrete hypotheses that practitioners can test.

The experiments are controlled and generally consistent with the theory’s qualitative predictions: moderate initial difficulty works best, larger question/answer budgets help, improvement saturates, and curriculum gains are largest for moderate adjacent difficulty gaps.
weaknesses: The main guarantees rely on very strong assumptions whose applicability to LLMs is not established. In particular, the finite and realizable model class assumption, exact empirical MLE update, and Assumption 4.3 linking per-question acceptance rates to global expected reward for almost all questions are substantial idealizations. The paper does not empirically validate these assumptions or estimate the constants that determine whether the bounds are non-vacuous.

The central curriculum result compares lower bounds, not actual expected rewards. A larger lower bound for easy-to-hard does not necessarily imply better model performance, and the baseline is only a uniform fixed mixture. This weakens the claimed practical force of the theorem.

The empirical evaluation is narrow: one synthetic shortest-path task, one small LLM, and mostly qualitative trend matching. There are no standard math/reasoning benchmarks, no comparison to broader curriculum strategies, and limited reporting of variance/significance beyond a few seeds.

The experiments are partly constructed to satisfy the theoretical setup, including controlled task partitions and CP-SAT selection to match initial Pass@1/difficulty assumptions. This is useful for validation but leaves unclear whether the conclusions transfer to natural task distributions.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The appendix gives useful dataset generation and LoRA hyperparameters, but there is no code release mentioned, limited detail on warm-up configurations, decoding settings, verifier implementation, random seeds, and exact data-selection tolerances.

The manuscript does not appear to include an explicit limitations or ethics discussion. The ethical risks are not severe for synthetic graph reasoning, but a limitations discussion would be important given the restrictive assumptions and narrow empirical scope.

Presentation is generally clear but mathematically dense, with important definitions deferred to the appendix and several claims described as matching simulations without enough quantitative detail. Some figures are hard to interpret from the text alone because axes/conditions are compactly described.

strengths: The paper tackles a timely question: why iterative generate-filter-finetune self-improvement can work, and when easy-to-hard curricula may help. A task-centric finite-sample framing is a useful angle relative to more population-level or dynamics-oriented prior theory.

The manuscript derives explicit lower-bound recursions that connect initialization quality, task difficulty, sample budget, and acceptance rate. Even if highly idealized, these recursions give interpretable qualitative predictions such as moderate task difficulty, budget dependence, and saturation.

The synthetic shortest-path experiments are aligned with the theoretical setting and include controlled variations of initial Pass@1, question budget, candidate budget, and difficulty separation. This is a reasonable first testbed for checking qualitative trends.
weaknesses: The central theoretical assumptions are very strong and insufficiently justified for LLM self-improvement. The finite realizable model class assumption, exact MLE over the class, filtered conditional distribution belonging to the class, and Assumption 4.3 relating per-question acceptance to global expected reward are all doing substantial work. The paper does not convincingly establish that these assumptions hold even approximately in the claimed LLM reasoning setting.

The main results are lower-bound comparisons, not direct guarantees that the easy-to-hard procedure obtains higher actual reward than the baseline. The paper repeatedly interprets tighter lower bounds as practical improvement, but this can be misleading when the bounds may be loose, vacuous, or dominated by proof artifacts.

The easy-to-hard theory depends on a model-invariant power-law ordering of task difficulties across all models in a neighborhood. This is a restrictive structural assumption, and the experiments appear to construct task partitions to satisfy the desired difficulty pattern rather than testing whether the condition naturally holds.

The empirical validation is too narrow for the strength of the claims. It uses one synthetic graph shortest-path task and one small model, with only qualitative trend matching. There are no real mathematical reasoning benchmarks, no comparisons to standard curriculum or self-training variants beyond a uniform mixture baseline, and limited statistical reporting beyond one standard-error band in one figure.

Some experimental design choices risk circularity. The authors select training and test sets to match target initial Pass@1 values, balance initially correct examples, and use CP-SAT to impose baseline and easy-to-hard partitions satisfying the theoretical difficulty constraints. This makes the experiments less convincing as independent validation of the theory.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The appendix gives some hyperparameters and dataset-generation details, but omits important information such as warm-up dataset sizes, exact warm-up configurations, sampling limits, CP-SAT formulation/tolerances, decoding settings, verifier details, seeds, and code. It would be difficult to reproduce the figures reliably from the manuscript alone.

Presentation is dense and often hard to audit. Key conditions such as M_i and N are deferred to the appendix and become algebraically elaborate, while the main text makes broad interpretive claims from them. There are also numerous typographical and formatting issues that make the theoretical statements and proofs harder to verify.

The limitations and ethics discussion is inadequate. The work is mostly theoretical and synthetic, so there are no obvious acute ethical concerns, but the manuscript should more clearly acknowledge that its assumptions and experiments do not yet establish practical guidance for real LLM self-improvement pipelines.

strengths: The paper offers a clear and useful finite-sample theory for iterative self-improvement, modeling each round as MLE on reward-filtered self-generated data and deriving explicit lower-bound dynamics that capture budget effects, moderate-difficulty regimes, and saturation.

The easy-to-hard curriculum analysis is a meaningful extension: the paper gives concrete feasibility and improvement conditions, and the resulting qualitative predictions are interpretable rather than purely formal.

The empirical section is well aligned with the theory. Controlled shortest-path experiments with Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct validate the predicted effects of initialization difficulty, question budget, answer budget, and adjacent task difficulty ratios.

Presentation is generally strong for a theory paper: notation is summarized, main conclusions are clearly connected to assumptions, and detailed proofs and experimental details are provided in the appendix.
No major ethical concerns are apparent, since the empirical work uses synthetic graph tasks and standard fine-tuning procedures.
weaknesses: The main guarantees rely on strong assumptions that limit external validity: finite realizable model class, positive essential infimum of acceptance rates, the reward-acceptance coupling in Assumption 4.3, and model-invariant power-law difficulty ordering in Assumption 5.1. These assumptions are plausible abstractions but not empirically checked in realistic LLM settings.

The empirical validation is narrow. Shortest-path graph reasoning is useful for control, but the paper’s motivation is mathematical/formal reasoning self-improvement; no real math, theorem proving, or broader reasoning benchmark is evaluated.

The comparison baseline is limited to a uniform fixed mixture. The paper does not compare against stronger adaptive curricula, hardness-aware sampling, or nonuniform mixtures, so the practical curriculum recommendation is less decisive.

Reproducibility is only partial. The appendix gives many details, but key items such as optimizer/scheduler details, CP-SAT selection specifics, exact seeds, full dataset construction scripts, and code availability are not evident from the manuscript.

The paper does not include a dedicated limitations section. While limitations can be inferred from the assumptions and experimental scope, an explicit discussion would make the claims easier to calibrate and reduce the risk of overgeneralizing the theory to production-scale self-improvement pipelines.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely question: why iterative rejection-sampling/self-improvement can work for verifiable reasoning tasks, and when easy-to-hard curricula should help.

The finite-sample perspective is a useful contribution. The single-task analysis makes explicit how acceptance rate, initialization quality, and sample budget interact, and it captures qualitative phenomena such as saturation and failures on tasks that are too easy or too hard.

The curriculum analysis is ambitious and gives interpretable sufficient conditions involving difficulty separation, initialization, and budget. Even if idealized, these conditions produce concrete qualitative predictions.

The empirical section is broader than many theory papers: it includes Monte Carlo illustrations, a synthetic shortest-path task with controlled difficulty, GSM8K, and DeepMind Mathematics across several model families and budgets.
Appendices provide detailed proofs and experimental hyperparameters, which helps readability and partial reproducibility.
weaknesses: The main theoretical guarantees rely on very strong assumptions whose connection to modern LLM fine-tuning is not established: finite and realizable model class, exact empirical MLE, accepted samples treated as i.i.d. from the filtered distribution, and a neighborhood Θ in which all iterates remain. These assumptions are central rather than cosmetic.

Assumption 4.3, which lower-bounds per-question acceptance rates by a multiple of the global expected reward except on a γ fraction of questions, is strong and not empirically checked. It rules out many heterogeneous reasoning distributions where a model solves some subpopulations and has near-zero probability on others, which is exactly a common LLM regime.

The curriculum theorem compares lower bounds, not actual expected rewards. A larger lower bound for easy-to-hard than for the baseline does not imply the easy-to-hard model has higher true performance, yet the presentation sometimes reads as if it explains actual curriculum superiority.

The empirical validation is mostly qualitative trend matching. The paper does not quantitatively test whether the theoretical conditions hold in the experiments, nor does it estimate key constants such as c, γ, |Π|, or the validity regions that drive the guarantees.

The synthetic setup may partly bake in the theory’s structure: task difficulty, initialization accuracy, and partitions are carefully constructed, including CP-SAT selection to satisfy desired properties. This supports illustration but weakens the claim that the theory explains natural self-improvement behavior.

The standard benchmark results are mixed. GSM8K gains are modest; small models degrade; DeepMind curriculum gains often have large standard errors; and Table 4 excludes modules with small β′ or small gap variation, which risks selection bias in the main evidence for moderate difficulty separation.

Reproducibility is incomplete: hyperparameters and prompts are given, but there is no apparent code release, exact dataset indices/partitions, compute details, decoding settings, verifier implementation, or full random-seed protocol sufficient to reproduce the controlled data construction and fine-tuning results.

The manuscript lacks an explicit limitations and ethics discussion. This is particularly relevant because self-generated training loops can amplify biases, benchmark contamination, or verifier-specific shortcuts, and because the theory’s assumptions are narrow relative to deployed LLM post-training.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely question: why iterative self-improvement with verifier-filtered samples can improve LLM reasoning, and when easy-to-hard curricula may help. A task-centric finite-sample framing is a useful angle relative to more population-level or model-dynamics accounts.

The manuscript contains substantial formal development. The single-step analysis, the multi-step lower-bound map, and the curriculum comparison identify intuitive factors such as initialization quality, accepted sample count, per-question sampling budget, and task difficulty separation.

The synthetic shortest-path experiments are well matched to the theory because they allow controlled variation of initial Pass@1, sample budget, answer budget, and difficulty separation. The observed qualitative trends are broadly consistent with the theoretical story.
The appendices provide many proof details and some implementation details, including prompt templates, LoRA hyperparameters, dataset construction, and seed averaging for the synthetic experiments.
weaknesses: The central theoretical assumptions are very strong and insufficiently justified for LLM self-improvement. The analysis assumes a finite model class, realizability of the reward-filtered conditional distribution in that class, global empirical MLE, a small neighborhood of parameters, and Assumption 4.3 linking per-question acceptance rates to average reward except on a small fraction of questions. These are not empirically checked, and some are quite implausible for modern LLM fine-tuning.

The guarantees are lower-bound comparisons, not direct guarantees of actual performance improvement. In particular, the easy-to-hard result proves that one lower bound is larger than another under complex sufficient conditions; this does not imply that the actual easy-to-hard model outperforms the fixed-mixture baseline. The paper often phrases trend agreement as validation, which overstates what the evidence supports.

The finite-sample bounds appear likely to be vacuous at realistic scale because they depend on quantities such as log |Pi|, ess inf acceptance probabilities, and constants c, gamma that are unknown and potentially poor for LLMs. The paper does not instantiate the bounds numerically on its experiments, so it is unclear whether the theory gives actionable predictions beyond qualitative intuition.

The curriculum assumptions are especially restrictive. Assumption 5.1 requires model-invariant power-law ordering of task difficulties over a parameter neighborhood. In the DeepMind experiments, beta and beta' are estimated only from the initialization model, not over the trajectory or a neighborhood, and the data construction in synthetic experiments explicitly enforces theory-friendly partitions.

The empirical evaluation is not convincing enough for the paper's claims. Standard benchmark gains are modest on GSM8K, sometimes negative for weaker models, and the easy-to-hard comparison is limited to DeepMind Mathematics modules after excluding modules with small beta' or small gap variation. Table 4 also shows several negative or non-monotone cases with large standard errors, but the discussion emphasizes supporting trends.

Baselines are narrow. The main comparison is against a uniform fixed mixture, whereas practical curriculum/self-improvement methods often use adaptive sampling, difficulty-balanced sampling, or acceptance-aware allocation. This weakens the significance of the claimed curriculum advantage.

Reproducibility is only partial. The paper gives prompts and hyperparameters, but does not appear to provide code, exact selected splits, CP-SAT constraints/solutions, decoding settings, verifier details, compute budget, or all random seeds. Given the constructed datasets and filtering process, these omissions matter.

The manuscript lacks an explicit limitations and ethics discussion. For this topic, limitations around verifier quality, distribution shift, contamination/memorization, compute cost, and risks of self-generated training loops should be addressed directly rather than only implicitly through remarks.

Presentation is mathematically dense and sometimes overconfident. The main text defers crucial definitions of Mi and N to the appendix, making the core theorem difficult to interpret, and the empirical claims use language such as 'validated' and 'closely match' where the evidence is mostly qualitative trend agreement.

strengths: The paper tackles a timely and important gap: a finite-sample, task-centric theory of iterative self-improvement for verifier-filtered LLM reasoning, including the role of easy-to-hard curricula. This is more practically aligned than purely population-level analyses, since it explicitly models accepted sample counts and finite question/answer budgets.

The main theoretical story is coherent and useful. The single-task analysis connects initialization quality, task difficulty, acceptance rates, sample size, and saturation; the curriculum analysis gives interpretable sufficient conditions involving difficulty separation, sample budget, and initialization. These results provide qualitative guidance that matches practitioner intuition but is made mathematically explicit.

The empirical validation is broader than is typical for a theory paper. The authors test predicted trends on a controllable synthetic shortest-path task and on standard mathematical reasoning benchmarks including GSM8K and DeepMind Mathematics, across multiple base models and budgets. The observed regimes of failure, improvement, saturation, and curriculum advantage generally support the theory.

Presentation is mostly strong. The paper clearly motivates the two central questions, separates assumptions from consequences, and gives interpretable remarks after technical results. The appendices include extensive proofs and implementation details, including dataset construction, prompts, LoRA hyperparameters, budgets, seeds for synthetic averages, and benchmark splits.

The work is original in its combination of finite-sample self-improvement guarantees with task difficulty/curriculum scheduling. Even where the method is not new empirically, the theoretical framing yields new understanding of when easy-to-hard scheduling should help.
weaknesses: The theory relies on strong assumptions whose empirical validity is only partially examined. In particular, the finite model class and realizability assumption in Theorem 4.1, the reward-acceptance coupling in Assumption 4.3, and the model-invariant power-law difficulty ordering in Assumption 5.1 are substantial idealizations. The experiments show trends consistent with the assumptions but do not directly estimate or stress-test all of them.

The guarantees are lower-bound comparisons under sufficient conditions, so the connection to actual performance is qualitative rather than tight. Several central curriculum conclusions are based on comparing bound sequences rather than proving direct dominance of the trained models, which should be emphasized more clearly as a limitation of the claims.

The empirical evidence for easy-to-hard curricula on real benchmarks is suggestive but not fully conclusive. Table 4 shows several modules where the fully staged or intermediate curriculum helps, but also negative or noisy cases; standard errors can be large, and the paper filters modules whose difficulty split or variation is small. This supports the theory’s trend but leaves open how robust the prescription is across broader tasks and less curated difficulty partitions.

Reproducibility is decent but incomplete. The manuscript provides prompts, hyperparameters, datasets, and construction procedures, but I did not see a code release statement. The CP-SAT data selection procedure and exact filtering criteria for some benchmark experiments may be hard to reproduce without code and exact random seeds for all reported runs.

The paper lacks an explicit limitations or ethics discussion. Ethical risks are not central for this theoretical/benchmark-focused work, but self-improvement pipelines can amplify verifier biases or benchmark-specific shortcuts, and the paper should more directly discuss these deployment and evaluation limitations.

Some presentation choices make the curriculum theory harder to digest than necessary. The main theorem defers key feasibility and improvement expressions to the appendix, and the notation-heavy conditions may limit accessibility for readers who want to apply the results. A compact worked example or diagnostic recipe would improve usability.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely question: why rejection-filtered iterative self-improvement can work in finite-sample regimes, and when easy-to-hard scheduling should help. The task-centric framing is useful and more aligned with math/reasoning pipelines than many abstract self-distillation analyses.

The theoretical development is coherent and reasonably substantial. The single-step bound makes explicit the role of accepted sample count, per-question acceptance rates, and answer budget m; the multi-step map gives a clear explanation for moderate-difficulty regimes and saturation; the curriculum analysis identifies interpretable levers such as adjacent difficulty separation, initialization, and sample budget.

The empirical section is well matched to the theory at the level of qualitative predictions. The synthetic shortest-path task gives controlled variation of initial Pass@1, question budget, answer budget, and difficulty separation, while the GSM8K and DeepMind Mathematics experiments show that several predicted trends also appear in standard reasoning benchmarks.

The appendix gives nontrivial proof detail and useful implementation information, including dataset construction, prompts, LoRA hyperparameters, budgets, and random-seed averaging for the synthetic experiments. The paper is generally readable despite a heavy mathematical load.
weaknesses: The central guarantees rely on strong idealizations whose practical validity is not established. In particular, the analysis assumes exact empirical MLE over a finite model class containing the reward-filtered conditional distribution, a small neighborhood of parameters, clean binary verification, and a strong lower-tail coupling condition between per-question acceptance and average reward. These assumptions are doing substantial work and are not empirically checked or calibrated for LLM fine-tuning.

The theory-to-experiment connection is mostly qualitative. The experiments verify trends such as larger budgets helping and moderate difficulty being best, but they do not estimate the constants or conditions in the theorems, test whether Assumptions 4.3/5.1 hold beyond initialization proxies, or compare predicted thresholds quantitatively against observed ones. As a result, the evidence supports the intuition more than the formal claims.

The experimental evaluation is somewhat selective. GSM8K gains are small for several models and negative for weak models; DeepMind Mathematics Table 2 uses easy modules with high initial performance; and the curriculum study filters modules based on beta and gap variation, which may bias toward observable curriculum effects. Stronger baselines and broader unfiltered reporting would make the empirical case more convincing.

Reproducibility is only partial. The paper reports prompts and major hyperparameters, but does not appear to provide code, exact optimizer/training details, decoding settings, hardware, seed lists, data-selection tolerances, or the CP-SAT formulation needed to reconstruct the synthetic and curriculum partitions. These omissions matter because the conclusions depend on carefully controlled data selection and iterative fine-tuning.

Limitations are discussed only briefly in the appendix, mainly around noisy rewards and test-time training. Important limitations such as verifier errors, exact-MLE mismatch, finite-class abstraction for neural LMs, selective benchmark construction, and potential data contamination or evaluation leakage are not foregrounded. There is also no explicit research ethics or broader-impact discussion, though the ethical risk is not central for this mostly theoretical work.

Presentation is dense and sometimes overclaims. Phrases such as empirical validation across diverse tasks are stronger than warranted by mostly trend-level evidence, and several key conditions are deferred to long expressions in the appendix, making it hard for readers to judge when the main theorem is meaningfully applicable.

strengths: The paper tackles a timely and relevant question: why iterative reward-filtered self-training can improve LLM reasoning, and when easy-to-hard curricula should help. A task-centric finite-sample perspective is a useful angle relative to population-only accounts.

The theoretical development is internally ambitious and attempts to connect single-task self-improvement, acceptance rates, sample budgets, saturation, and curriculum scheduling in one framework. The feedback-loop interpretation is intuitive and potentially valuable.

The experiments cover both a controlled synthetic shortest-path task and standard math benchmarks, and several observed trends are plausible: larger sampling budgets help, gains saturate, and curricula can be beneficial at moderate difficulty gaps.
The appendix provides substantial proof material and some experimental details, including prompts, LoRA hyperparameters, and dataset construction procedures.
weaknesses: The soundness of the main claims is limited by very strong and largely unvalidated assumptions. The finite model class and realizability assumption that the reward-filtered conditional distribution lies in the model class are not credible for LLM fine-tuning, and the paper does not show how the constants or conditions map to real models.

Assumption 4.3 is central but very strong: it requires most per-question success probabilities to be lower-bounded by a constant times average performance. This excludes precisely the heterogeneous reasoning settings where some instances are much harder than others, yet the empirical validation does not test whether the assumption holds.

The curriculum theory rests on Assumption 5.1, which requires model-invariant power-law difficulty ratios over a neighborhood of fine-tuned models. This is neither empirically verified nor convincingly justified; estimating beta and beta prime from the initialization model in Figure 5 is not evidence that the assumption holds across training.

Several theoretical guarantees are lower-bound comparisons rather than performance guarantees for actual training. Showing that the easy-to-hard lower bound exceeds the baseline lower bound does not imply the actual easy-to-hard model outperforms the actual baseline, and the paper often presents this as stronger practical guidance than the math supports.

The experimental design is partly circular. In the synthetic setting, datasets are selected to match desired initial Pass@1 values and, for curriculum experiments, to satisfy the paper's own assumption using a CP-SAT construction. This makes the experiments less an independent validation of the theory than a controlled demonstration under engineered conditions.

The standard benchmark evidence is weak. GSM8K results are low and mixed for weaker models, DeepMind Mathematics uses selected easy modules or filtered modules, and Table 4 excludes modules with small beta prime or small gap variation. This selection can exaggerate support for the claimed curriculum pattern.

Statistical support is insufficient. Many tables report single trajectories with no standard deviations or significance tests, while Table 4 includes standard errors but many claimed positive gaps are small, noisy, or non-monotone. The paper does not convincingly establish that the trends are robust.

Reproducibility is incomplete. There is no code release information, no compute budget, limited seed reporting, insufficient detail on answer extraction/normalization and verification, and only high-level description of the CP-SAT dataset selection. Reproducing the results would likely require substantial guesswork.

The limitations discussion is too narrow. It mentions noisy rewards and test-time training only briefly, but does not adequately discuss the unrealistic verifier assumptions, selection bias in experimental construction, mismatch between theory and LLM optimization, or risks of over-interpreting sufficient lower-bound conditions.

Presentation is dense and difficult to follow. Key definitions such as the feasibility and improvement conditions are deferred, the paper contains many long algebraic expressions with limited intuition, and there are noticeable formatting/typographical issues. The main contribution would benefit from a much clearer statement of what is actually proved versus empirically suggested.

Originality is moderate rather than high. The paper combines known ingredients: rejection-sampled self-training, finite-sample MLE bounds, and curriculum difficulty scheduling. The synthesis is interesting, but the central assumptions and empirical validation are not strong enough to make the contribution convincing for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important question: why iterative self-improvement with reward-filtered model-generated data can work, and when easy-to-hard curricula help. The task-centric framing is useful and better aligned with practical reasoning pipelines than purely population-level or continuous-dynamics views.

The main theoretical contribution is substantive. The finite-sample analysis exposes an intuitive feedback loop in which better models accept more samples, yielding improved effective sample sizes, while also explaining saturation. The extension to curricula gives concrete sufficient conditions involving initialization, sample budget, and difficulty separation.

The empirical section is well matched to the theory. The synthetic shortest-path task allows controlled variation of initialization difficulty, question budget, answer budget, and difficulty ratios, and the observed trends largely support the theoretical predictions. The GSM8K and DeepMind Mathematics experiments provide additional evidence beyond the synthetic setting.

Presentation is generally clear despite the technical density. The paper states assumptions explicitly, defers long expressions to the appendix, includes algorithmically relevant experimental details, and provides useful qualitative interpretations of the theorem conditions.

The limitations discussion is honest: the authors acknowledge the clean verifier assumption and the gap to noisy reward settings and test-time compute methods. This is appropriate and should not be penalized.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees rely on strong assumptions whose practical validity is only partially justified. In particular, the finite model class/realizability assumption, the positive reward-acceptance coupling in Assumption 4.3, and the model-invariant power-law difficulty ordering in Assumption 5.1 are substantial restrictions; the paper does not empirically test how well these assumptions hold in the LLM experiments.

The results are mainly qualitative validations of predicted trends rather than tight quantitative confirmations of the bounds. The bounds involve constants and conditions that are difficult to estimate for real models, so it remains unclear how predictive the theory is beyond explaining observed phenomena after the fact.

The empirical evaluation is useful but limited in scope. Most controlled experiments use a small Llama-3.2-1B model on a synthetic graph task, and the standard benchmark experiments mostly report self-improvement trajectories rather than comparisons to stronger curriculum/self-training baselines from the literature.

The easy-to-hard experiments on DeepMind Mathematics involve filtering modules based on measurable curriculum effects and difficulty split criteria. This is reasonable for analysis, but it may overstate how consistently the curriculum advantage appears across the full benchmark distribution.

Reproducibility is only moderate. The paper gives prompts, hyperparameters, and data construction details, but it does not clearly state code release, exact random seeds for all tables, full partition files, compute budget, or enough implementation detail to exactly reproduce the CP-SAT dataset selection and fine-tuning runs.

The originality is meaningful but not exceptional: the paper combines known elements of rejection-sampling self-improvement, finite-sample MLE analysis, and curriculum learning. The main novelty is the task-centric finite-sample synthesis and curriculum analysis, rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic method.
